Electromagnetic Waves & Radiation

Light as a field phenomenon

← PSE II Course

31.0 — The Greatest Prediction in Physics

In the mid-19th century, James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879) accomplished something extraordinary. He took the experimental discoveries of four physicists — Coulomb’s law of electric force, Gauss’s observation that electric flux counts enclosed charge, Faraday’s discovery that changing magnetic fields produce electric fields, and Ampère’s law relating magnetic fields to currents — and unified them into a single mathematical framework. In the process, he discovered that the equations predicted something no one had observed: self-sustaining waves of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, propagating through empty space at a speed determined entirely by two laboratory-measured constants.

That speed turned out to be the speed of light.

“We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.” — James Clerk Maxwell, 1864

Maxwell did not live to see his prediction verified experimentally. It was Heinrich Hertz (1857–1894) who, in 1887, constructed an oscillating circuit to produce electromagnetic waves and a separate circuit to detect them. By measuring the wavelength and frequency of the detected signal, Hertz confirmed that the waves traveled at \(c\) — exactly as Maxwell had predicted. The unit of frequency, the hertz (Hz = cycles/second), honors this achievement.

*Personal note: Maxwell’s unification of electricity, magnetism, and light is arguably the single greatest intellectual achievement in the history of physics — perhaps in the history of science. He took four separate empirical laws, discovered a missing symmetry (the displacement current), and predicted an entirely new phenomenon. Einstein kept a portrait of Maxwell on his study wall. When asked if he stood on Newton’s shoulders, Einstein replied: “No, I stand on Maxwell’s shoulders.”

31.1 — Maxwell’s Equations

The four equations that govern all electromagnetic phenomena are:

1. Gauss’s Law for Electricity (Ch 23):

\[\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_\text{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}\]

Electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by \(\varepsilon_0\). Field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges.

2. Gauss’s Law for Magnetism:

\[\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0\]

Magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. Field lines form continuous loops — no magnetic monopoles exist.

3. Faraday’s Law (Ch 29):

\[\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}\]

A changing magnetic flux induces a circulating electric field. The minus sign (Lenz’s law) ensures the induced field opposes the change.

4. Ampère-Maxwell Law:

\[\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s} = \mu_0 I_\text{enc} + \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\]

A circulating magnetic field is produced by current and by a changing electric flux. The second term — the displacement current \(I_d = \varepsilon_0 \, d\Phi_E/dt\) — is Maxwell’s addition. It completes the symmetry: a changing \(\vec{B}\) creates \(\vec{E}\) (Faraday), and a changing \(\vec{E}\) creates \(\vec{B}\) (Maxwell).

The Symmetry

Electric Magnetic
Source Charges (\(Q\)) Moving charges / currents (\(I\))
Flux law \(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = Q/\varepsilon_0\) \(\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0\)
Circulation law \(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s} = -d\Phi_B/dt\) \(\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s} = \mu_0 I + \mu_0\varepsilon_0 \, d\Phi_E/dt\)
What creates it Charges or changing \(\vec{B}\) Currents or changing \(\vec{E}\)

The near-perfect symmetry between the third and fourth equations is what makes electromagnetic waves possible: a changing \(\vec{E}\) creates \(\vec{B}\), which in turn changes and creates more \(\vec{E}\), which creates more \(\vec{B}\) — an endless, self-sustaining oscillation that propagates through space.

31.2 — The Displacement Current

Maxwell’s key insight was recognizing a gap in Ampère’s original law. Consider a capacitor being charged by a current \(I\). Choose an Amperian loop around the wire: Ampère’s law gives \(\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s} = \mu_0 I\). Now stretch the surface bounded by the same loop so it passes between the capacitor plates, where no charge flows. The current through this surface is zero — yet the magnetic field around the wire hasn’t changed!

The resolution: between the plates, the electric field is changing as charge accumulates. Maxwell defined the displacement current:

\[\boxed{I_d = \varepsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt}}\]

This is not a real current — no charges move between the plates. But a changing electric flux produces the same magnetic effect as a real current. Adding \(I_d\) to Ampère’s law restores consistency: the magnetic field around the loop is the same regardless of which surface you choose.

*Personal note: The displacement current is perhaps the most consequential theoretical addition in physics. It is not demanded by any experiment Maxwell had access to — he added it purely for mathematical consistency (the divergence of the curl must be zero). From this act of theoretical hygiene, the entire theory of electromagnetic waves followed. Symmetry and mathematical consistency, not experiment, led to the prediction of light.

31.3 — Electromagnetic Waves

The Wave Prediction

With the displacement current in place, Maxwell’s equations in free space (no charges, no currents) become perfectly symmetric: a changing \(\vec{E}\) creates \(\vec{B}\), and a changing \(\vec{B}\) creates \(\vec{E}\). Maxwell showed that these coupled equations yield a wave equation for both fields. The solution describes transverse waves — oscillating \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\) fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation.

The speed of these waves depends only on two constants measurable in the laboratory:

\[\boxed{c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}}\]

Substituting \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2/(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2)\):

\[c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi \times 10^{-7})(8.854 \times 10^{-12})}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1.113 \times 10^{-17}}} = 2.998 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}\]

This is the speed of light — measured independently by Fizeau, Foucault, and others. Maxwell’s equations, built from electrostatics and magnetostatics experiments, predict the speed of light without any reference to optics. The conclusion is inescapable: light is an electromagnetic wave.

Properties of EM Waves

The electric and magnetic fields in an EM wave are related by:

\[\boxed{\frac{E}{B} = c}\]

Since \(c \approx 3 \times 10^8\) m/s, the electric field amplitude is vastly larger than the magnetic field amplitude in SI units. Both fields oscillate in phase — they reach their maxima and minima at the same points in space and time.

The wave obeys the standard wave relation:

\[c = f\lambda\]

where \(f\) is the frequency (Hz) and \(\lambda\) is the wavelength (m). Since \(c\) is constant in vacuum, higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

Key properties of electromagnetic waves:

  • Transverse: \(\vec{E}\), \(\vec{B}\), and the propagation direction are mutually perpendicular
  • Self-sustaining: No medium required — EM waves propagate through vacuum
  • Speed: All EM waves travel at \(c\) in vacuum, regardless of frequency
  • Generated by: Any accelerating charge radiates electromagnetic waves

31.4 — Energy Transport: The Poynting Vector

Electromagnetic waves carry energy. The rate of energy transport per unit area is described by the Poynting vector:

\[\boxed{\vec{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0} \vec{E} \times \vec{B}}\]

The direction of \(\vec{S}\) is the direction of wave propagation (perpendicular to both \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\)), and its magnitude gives the intensity — the power per unit area (W/m²).

Since \(E\) and \(B\) oscillate sinusoidally, the time-averaged intensity is:

\[\boxed{I = S_\text{avg} = \frac{E_0 B_0}{2\mu_0} = \frac{c\varepsilon_0 E_0^2}{2} = \frac{c B_0^2}{2\mu_0}}\]

where \(E_0\) and \(B_0\) are the maximum field amplitudes. The three equivalent forms follow from \(E_0 = cB_0\) and \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\).

Example: Intensity of Sunlight

The average intensity of sunlight at Earth’s surface is approximately \(I = 1400\ \text{W/m}^2\). What is the maximum electric field strength?

\[E_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2I}{c\varepsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(1400)}{(3.00 \times 10^8)(8.854 \times 10^{-12})}} = \sqrt{\frac{2800}{2.656 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{1.054 \times 10^{6}}\]

\[\boxed{E_0 = 1030\ \text{V/m}}\]

And the corresponding magnetic field:

\[B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c} = \frac{1030}{3.00 \times 10^8} = 3.42 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{T} = 3.42\ \mu\text{T}\]

The electric field of sunlight is about 1 kV/m — comparable to the field near a charged capacitor. The magnetic field is only a few microtesla — far weaker than Earth’s magnetic field (~50 μT). This illustrates why the electric field dominates most light-matter interactions.

Example: A Radio Station

A radio station broadcasts at \(P = 50.0\ \text{kW}\). Assuming the signal radiates uniformly in all directions, find the electric field amplitude at a distance of \(r = 10.0\ \text{km}\).

The power spreads over the surface of a sphere:

\[I = \frac{P}{4\pi r^2} = \frac{5.00 \times 10^4}{4\pi (1.00 \times 10^4)^2} = \frac{5.00 \times 10^4}{1.257 \times 10^9} = 3.98 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{W/m}^2\]

Then:

\[E_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2I}{c\varepsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(3.98 \times 10^{-5})}{(3.00 \times 10^8)(8.854 \times 10^{-12})}} = \sqrt{\frac{7.96 \times 10^{-5}}{2.656 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{0.02996}\]

\[\boxed{E_0 = 0.173\ \text{V/m}}\]

Compare this to the sunlight result: 1030 V/m at Earth’s surface versus 0.173 V/m from a powerful radio station at 10 km. Sunlight is about 6000× stronger — yet your radio antenna picks up the station just fine, because the receiver is tuned to amplify a specific frequency via resonance.

*Personal note: The intensity falls off as \(1/r^2\) from the source — the same inverse-square law that governs Coulomb’s force (Chapter 22). Energy spreads over the surface of an expanding sphere (\(A = 4\pi r^2\)), so the power per unit area decreases as the square of the distance. The same geometry, the same mathematics, the same physics.

31.5 — The Electromagnetic Spectrum

Maxwell predicted that electromagnetic waves could exist at any frequency — visible light is merely the narrow band to which human eyes are sensitive. The full electromagnetic spectrum spans over 20 orders of magnitude in frequency:

Region Frequency Range Wavelength Range Sources / Applications
Radio \(< 300\) MHz \(> 1\) m AM/FM radio, TV, MRI
Microwave 300 MHz – 300 GHz 1 mm – 1 m Radar, ovens, cell phones, Wi-Fi
Infrared 300 GHz – 400 THz 750 nm – 1 mm Thermal radiation, remote controls, night vision
Visible 400 – 750 THz 400 – 750 nm Human vision
Ultraviolet 750 THz – 30 PHz 10 – 400 nm Sun, sterilization, fluorescence
X-ray 30 PHz – 30 EHz 0.01 – 10 nm Medical imaging, crystallography
Gamma ray \(> 30\) EHz \(< 0.01\) nm Nuclear decay, cosmic sources

All of these are the same phenomenon — oscillating electric and magnetic fields propagating at \(c\) — differing only in frequency. The boundaries between regions are conventional, not physical.

Key relationships:

\[c = f\lambda \qquad E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\]

The second equation (the Planck relation) connects the wave description to the particle description: each photon carries energy \(E = hf\), where \(h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J}\cdot\text{s}\) is Planck’s constant. Higher frequency means higher energy per photon — this is why gamma rays are dangerous and radio waves are harmless.

Common wavelengths and frequencies:

Color \(\lambda\) (nm) \(f\) (THz)
Red 700 428
Orange 600 500
Yellow 580 517
Green 530 566
Blue 470 638
Violet 400 750

*Personal note: The visible spectrum — the entire range of colors the human eye can detect — spans less than one octave in frequency (a factor of ~1.8 from red to violet). Compare this to hearing, which spans roughly 10 octaves (20 Hz to 20 kHz). We see an astonishingly narrow slice of the electromagnetic world.

31.6 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Maxwell’s equations — four equations that unify electricity, magnetism, and light. The displacement current (\(I_d = \varepsilon_0 \, d\Phi_E/dt\)) completes the symmetry.
  2. A changing \(\vec{E}\) creates \(\vec{B}\), and a changing \(\vec{B}\) creates \(\vec{E}\) — this mutual induction produces self-sustaining electromagnetic waves.
  3. EM waves travel at \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = 3.00 \times 10^8\) m/s in vacuum.
  4. EM waves are transverse: \(\vec{E} \perp \vec{B} \perp\) propagation, with \(E/B = c\).
  5. The Poynting vector \(\vec{S} = (1/\mu_0)\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\) gives the direction and rate of energy transport.
  6. The electromagnetic spectrum spans radio to gamma rays — all the same phenomenon at different frequencies.
  7. Photon energy is \(E = hf\) — higher frequency means higher energy.

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Speed of light \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = 3.00 \times 10^8\) m/s
Wave relation \(c = f\lambda\)
Field ratio \(E/B = c\)
Displacement current \(I_d = \varepsilon_0 \, d\Phi_E/dt\)
Poynting vector \(\vec{S} = (1/\mu_0)\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\)
Average intensity \(I = c\varepsilon_0 E_0^2/2\)
Photon energy \(E = hf = hc/\lambda\)

Maxwell’s Equations

Equation Name What It Says
\(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = Q/\varepsilon_0\) Gauss (E) Charges create diverging E fields
\(\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0\) Gauss (B) No magnetic monopoles
\(\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s} = -d\Phi_B/dt\) Faraday Changing B creates circulating E
\(\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s} = \mu_0(I + \varepsilon_0 \, d\Phi_E/dt)\) Ampère-Maxwell Current or changing E creates circulating B

Looking Ahead

In Chapters 28 and 29, we will study the magnetic fields and electromagnetic induction that Maxwell’s equations describe. We will see how magnetic forces act on charges and currents, how Faraday’s law produces EMFs in circuits, and how inductors store energy in magnetic fields. The story will culminate in LC oscillations — electrical circuits that oscillate at a natural frequency \(\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}\), converting energy between electric and magnetic fields in the same way that Maxwell’s equations predict electromagnetic waves convert energy between \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\) in free space.
